title: The Oral History Is a Succession Document
author: RN Collins
principle: Evidence leads; atmosphere never substitutes for provenance.

narrativeSequence.caption: Oral history becomes succession infrastructure when it preserves decision context, contradiction, sensory judgment, relationships, boundaries, and the narrator’s authority over access and use.
One frame holds a named designer, a model, a photographer, a collection, and an institutional record—separate roles that public shorthand often compresses.

narrativeSequence.caption: 01 · PREPARE — Who should speak and under what conditions?. Define purpose, interviewer, narrator, consent, accessibility, language, compensation, privacy, cultural authority, distress protocol, topics declined, recording ownership, and withdrawal limits.

narrativeSequence.caption: 02 · ELICIT — Which decisions cannot be read from files?. Ask for sensory thresholds, rejected options, relationship dynamics, exceptions, informal vocabulary, moments of uncertainty, and what the narrator does not know.

narrativeSequence.caption: 03 · CORRECT — Can narrators revise the record?. Provide transcript, contextual notes, name and pronoun checks, redaction, embargo, restriction, disagreement, and approval choices without promising control the archive cannot legally grant.
